title: Gromit Speaks: Martin Freeman to Voice Beloved but Mute Dog in Audiobook Edition of Autobiography

body:
He’s been one half of one of the most cherished on-screen duos in history, yet has famously never spoken a word. That is, up until now. 

	Gromit, the whip-smart and eye-rolling four-legged friend to cheese-loving inventor Wallace across numerous stop-motion classics from Aardman Animation and “Wallace & Gromit” creator Nick Park, is getting his first autobiography and, with it, an audiobook. 


	In step Martin Freeman, who will narrate “Grand: The Autobiography of Gromit, as Told to Nick Park,” a book in which, according to the description, Gromit “finally breaks his silence.”
	

	“When you create a character who has no voice, and whose facial expressions are everything, what do you do when your publisher reminds you there’ll be an audiobook? Who could possibly be the voice of a character everyone feels they know, but nobody’s actually heard?” said Park, winner of four Oscars, including three for Wallace & Gromit films “The Wrong Trousers,” “A Close Shave” and “The Curse of the Were-Rabbit.”


	“The more I thought about it, the more I realised Martin Freeman was the obvious choice really. I was genuinely thrilled and honoured when he said yes.”

	Recording took place earlier this month at Penguin Studios, with both “Grand: The Autobiography of Gromit” and the audiobook now due for release Oct. 22.

	But Park, having previously stated that Freeman was “the voice” of Gromit, in almost the same breath attempted to (doggy) walk back the de-muting of his plasticine hound. 

	“Martin is not doing a Gromit ‘voice’ as such,” he said. “He’s reading Gromit’s story as Gromit put it; his inner thoughts, his candid insights and endless witticisms, bringing to them his usual colour, thoughtfulness and wry humour.” now from all major audiobook retailers.

schema.headline: Gromit Speaks: Martin Freeman to Voice Beloved but Mute Dog in Audiobook Edition of Autobiography

title: Margherita Ferrari on Working With Paolo Sorrentino on Directorial Debut ‘Föa — Once Upon a Future’: ‘He Helped Me Pursue and Protect My Vision’
description: Debuting Italian director Margherita Ferrari is at the Busan International Film Festival with “Föa – Once Upon a Future,” an innovative coming-of-ag
body:
Debuting Italian director Margherita Ferrari is at the Busan International Film Festival with “Föa – Once Upon a Future,” an innovative coming-of-age drama that also marks Paolo Sorrentino‘s debut as a producer.

	Set in Genoa during the tragic days in July 2001 when the G8 summit led to deathly clashes between protesters and police, “Once Upon a Future” tells the story of Nicole, an 18-year-old girl who is eight months pregnant and takes three protesters into her home. Using a fable-like tone, the film provides a fresh perspective on the G8 violence that became a watershed moment in the anti-globalization movement.
	

	“’Föa’ begins with a wound that history never quite managed to close,” Sorrentino said in a statement to Variety. “Margherita Ferrari turns the memory of Genoa into something intimate and dreamlike, where the past quietly returns to question the future.”


	“Föa – Once Upon a Future,” which stars emerging talents Gaia Ravina, Clara Tramontano, Iker Urgoiti and Gabriele Falsetta, was co-produced by Sorrentino′s production company Numero 10, with The Apartment and PiperFilm. PiperPlay is handling international sales.

	“At a time when imagination needs to be protected, supporting new authors and their singular visions feels more important than ever,” Sorrentino continued. “I am particularly proud that Numero 10 begins this journey with a film told through such a powerful female gaze — a story that reminds us that even after the future seems to have disappeared, it may still be waiting for us.”

	The film started as Ferrari’s graduation short at Rome’s Centro Sperimentale film school, after which she had the opportunity to pitch the expanded project to Sorrentino. Below, Ferrari speaks to Variety about what sparked “Once Upon a Future” creatively and its fortuitous production journey.
	
	
		How did the “Föa – Once Upon a Future” story germinate?	

	On July 20, 2001, I was only 4. I remember the windows and the typical green shutters of our living room in Genoa had to be closed because outside there was smoke and noise. So, even though it was summer and sweltering inside, we had to barricade ourselves in, staying in the dark. Shut away. That image came back to me during the pandemic. I had sought out that same feeling — of solitude, isolation and even powerlessness — while something much bigger than me and all of us, something powerfully collective, was happening outside. On a more personal level, I’ve always felt a certain disillusionment regarding the limits of my own power; how little impact I can actually have on the world or on contemporary reality. It’s a feeling that hits me every time I speak about this subject.
	
		Tell me more.	

	I know I’m not just talking about me. I see this reflected in so many of my peers, and perhaps in people in general, who are experiencing the world as it is today. So there is that, combined with the lingering wound of those days and all the traces they left behind. Speaking as someone from Genoa, I felt a desire to tell a story that, even though it’s set in 2001, is really about the future and about today. How do you do that? Usually, fairy tales are set in the distant past. Yet they’re actually meant to speak to the present. So, that’s more or less how it all came about.
	
		Starting with the title, “Föa – Once Upon a Future,” this film is a fable of sorts. Talk to me about this narrative choice, which is unusual in dealing with historical fact.	

	The Genoese term “Föa” actually means “story,” in the sense of a made-up story, a little tale or a fable. That aspect interested us [myself and my co-writers] partly because we wanted to blend history with a capital H, the kind you study in books, with a fictional tale about a character who doesn’t exist. It also suggests that to tell the truth about reality, you somehow need invention and metaphors, and therefore cinema and fables too. We also wanted to approach this historical event from a more emotional, dreamlike perspective, focusing on the almost unconscious traces that were left within us by those days. This applies even to those, like us, who experienced the aftermath of the Genoa G8 events. In a way, we always felt like we were inside Nicole’s womb, so to speak. The child Nicole is carrying in the film would be 25 or 26 years old today. In a sense, he has been carrying the same question we have, which is: “What will the future awaiting us actually be like?”
	

	I’d like to add that I hope this film offers more than just the questions that are raised by those events. I hope it allows the audience to imagine that things might turn out a bit better. It’s like in fairy tales, I always envisioned a moment of relief at the end, a breath of fresh air that leaves room for that possibility. 
	
		What was it like to have Paolo Sorrentino as your producer?	

	Paolo was very involved during both the initial writing phase and the editing process. But not on set. He treaded lightly in that phase. He just stopped by once to say hello. I tried to get him involved, but he didn’t want to. Basically, he was very keen on not being intrusive and to respect the boundaries of the set. I view that gesture as an act of great tenderness on his part. Even though I’ve always loved getting his advice, it never scared me, I find Paolo to be very patient. I think he had often already thought out certain solutions before we did. But he waited for me, or for me and the editor, to get there on our own, to reach the direction in which the film needed to go. He helped me pursue and protect my vision all the way to the end, while supporting my work as a director through every single phase. It was a beautiful creative process from the start. It also helped me grow, helped me bring the film to the screen and become the person I am today. That’s more or less how it went.



	

									Courtesy PiperPlay

schema.headline: Margherita Ferrari on Working With Paolo Sorrentino on Directorial Debut ‘Föa — Once Upon a Future’: ‘He Helped Me Pursue and Protect My Vision’

title: UTA and Gold House Set Partnership to Build Asia-Hollywood Bridge (EXCLUSIVE)
description: UTA and Gold House are joining forces at the Busan International Film Festival and in Seoul this month, marking the Asian Pacific advocacy organizat
body:
UTA and Gold House are joining forces at the Busan International Film Festival and in Seoul this month, marking the Asian Pacific advocacy organization’s first official foray into Korea as the two look to connect Asian creatives and investors with Hollywood.

	The partnership kicks off with the UTA x Gold House x Variety Industry Night at the Park Hyatt on Friday (Oct. 9). The two companies will then stage a panel, “Hollywood & the Asian Diaspora,” at the Asian Contents & Film Market on Oct. 10, before moving to Seoul on Oct. 13 for a speakeasy party for cross-cultural creatives, funders and founders.
	

	David Park, a senior partner and agent at UTA, notes that the agency has worked in Asia, particularly Korea and Japan, for several years. “Adding Gold House has allowed us to level up, quite frankly,” he says.


	Until now, Gold House’s formal footprint in Asia had been limited to Singapore and Taiwan. Christine Yi, executive VP and president, Gold House Studios., is of Korean heritage, as is Daniel Suh, who runs the organization’s venture capital fund. The pair made an exploratory trip to Korea around this time last year to meet people in the local industry and ask what role Gold House could play.

	“What we had heard the most about was, do the Gold House thing here. You don’t really have to reinvent the wheel,” Yi says. “Especially as it relates to bringing major Hollywood executives, Dave included, to the table in order to really help facilitate more cross-border partnership, that’s something that they would really want from us.”
	

	“I don’t know if 2026 is the right moment, honestly. The right moment would have been sometime in the past, so I would say that we’re actually overdue,” Yi adds, pointing to Gold House’s investments in Korean startups and the number of its investors based in the country.

	Neither side has a formal, ongoing program in place yet. Gold House launched Gold House Studios, its in-house production arm, this year, and Yi plans to use the Korea trip to meet creatives the company wants to work with. “The partnership to us is really all about network and ecosystem building,” she says.

	On what they look for in Asian talent and IP, both point to authenticity. “Specificity is what leads to success,” Yi says. “Audiences can tell when something has been watered down for a global palate, and that’s not what they’re asking for.”

	Projects needn’t be in English, she adds, but they must connect with English-speaking audiences, where Gold House’s audience base sits. The company’s track record also leans heavily on first features, a stage where filmmakers “need someone to really take a bet on them.”

	Yi is also eyeing Korean talent-led projects. She won’t name names, but says a singer from a group that would come up “within your first couple” if one listed the top K-pop acts in the world has approached Gold House about making a film.

	“She can call anybody at all. But I think the way that her team wanted to approach us is like, ‘You guys might not be exactly the people, for whatever reason. However, we trust that you know who the right people are if it is not you, and to help us really navigate the U.S.,’” Yi says. “That’s a super-intimidating ask, especially when you’re coming in in a new medium that audiences might not necessarily associate with you.”

	Gold House hopes to guide the strategy and possibly work on the production, and Yi sees overseas talent looking for “a safe place to land” as a pipeline worth exploring while in Korea.

	Park’s touchstones for authenticity include “Parasite,” whose upstairs-downstairs class story landed in France, and “KPop Demon Hunters,” from his client Maggie Kang. “The only regret she has is that she didn’t add more Korean into the lyrics of some of the songs, or more actual specific locations that she wanted to bring into it,” he says, describing it as a balance Kang had to strike with Sony Pictures and Netflix.
	

	He would also like to see Korea tackle horror comedy. “Comedy is so culturally subjective, it’s harder to travel. But when embedded so intricately and so deeply with horror, for example, that could work, and it could be a huge hit,” Park says.

	One of the biggest gaps in the Asia-Hollywood pipeline, in Park’s view, is a shortage of crossover producers with a base in Asia and relationships with L.A. buyers. Outside Netflix and Disney, which run local teams, most buyers rely on U.S. headquarters to judge premium local-language content. “I probably can, if I had to, list those people on one hand,” he says.

	For Yi, one gap is capital. She is keen to see whether Asia-based private investors would back U.S. independent films, an asset class she says many individuals in U.S. indie film treat “like philanthropy.” She is also scouting Korean unscripted producing partners.

	Looking further ahead, Yi wants to build a cross-border talent development program, whether an exchange, a shadowing scheme or an accelerator.

	Park is on board, noting that Bong Joon Ho and “Squid Game” creator Hwang Dong-hyuk can now stay in Seoul and still win Oscars and Emmys. He points to his client Na Hong-Jin, whose “Hope” he calls the biggest movie out of Korea. “Identifying him before he did ‘The Wailing’ would be incredible,” Park says.

	Gold House has an executive producer role on Stephanie Ahn’s “Bedford Park,” which is screening at the festival.

title: ‘Celeste’ Creator Diego San José, Director Elena Trapé on Turning a Tax Inspector Into ‘Dirty Harry’
description: After turning Spain’s tax agency into the unlikely engine of a noir-tinged comedy, “Celeste” creator Diego San José and director Elena Trapé are tak
body:
After turning Spain’s tax agency into the unlikely engine of a noir-tinged comedy, “Celeste” creator Diego San José and director Elena Trapé are taking aim at something far more sacred in Spain: soccer.

	The six-part second season of the Movistar Plus original brings Carmen Machi (“La Mesías”) back as Sara Santano, the tax inspector who spent Season 1 trying to prove that a globe-trotting Latin music star owed €20 million ($22.4 million) in Spain. This time round, the series rewinds to an earlier point in Sara’s career and revisits Figueroa, the Argentine soccer star whose earlier tax case marked the only professional failure of Sara’s otherwise distinguished career.
	

	The social equation flips with him. Sara embodies one of Spain’s least-loved public figures; Figueroa is a soccer idol whose failings can be forgiven as long as he delivers on the pitch.


	Imagina Sales (The Mediapro Studio Distribution) is handling international sales on Season 2 and will bring the series to Mipcom ahead of its Oct. 26 world premiere at Barcelona’s Serielizados Fest.

	Season 1 won Spain’s Ondas and Feroz awards for best comedy, while Series Mania’s International Panorama awarded it best series and best actress for Machi last year. It also launched on Arte in France and Flow in Argentina.

	Produced by Movistar Plus and 100 Balas, and The Mediapro Studio company, the new season is again directed by Trapé, with San José writing alongside Oriol Puig and Fernando Delgado-Hierro.

	San José and Trapé spoke to Variety ahead of Mipcom about the new season.
	

	Why make Season 2 a prequel and return to the Figueroa case?

	San José: It really has nothing to do with the person she is pursuing. The decision to go back in time had to do with Sara Santano herself. The Sara we leave at the end of the first season is a woman whose wounds have healed. For a writer, that’s not the most interesting version of her. We wanted a character with wounds and cracks.

	So we went back to Figueroa as an excuse to go back to Sara. The case is really a pretext. The advantage of Figueroa isn’t Figueroa. It’s that her husband is alive. That allows us to tell a completely different personal story.

	If the first season is about solitude, the second is about the end of love — what happens when two people sleep separately, still care for one another, but are no longer in love.

	When you were making Season 1, had you already planted the Figueroa case with a second season in mind?

	San José: No. Everything to do with making a second season came after the first was already finished. So at the writing stage we had to approach it almost as an exercise in architecture, or juggling. The first challenge was to make a good season even for somebody who hasn’t seen the first one, so the story works simply as a story.

	Then we set ourselves another challenge: making sure everything fits and resonates. If somebody watches both seasons and takes out a magnifying glass looking for something that doesn’t fit, they shouldn’t find it. We also wanted Season 2 to help explain things from the first that were already there.

	Sara is exemplary, but she also breaks her own rules. What interests you about pushing her across those lines?

	San José: Stories become interesting when characters do things they don’t normally do. Sara is an exemplary inspector, but we put her in circumstances where she breaks her own rules.

	She is as obsessive and methodical as an FBI agent looking for a serial killer in Manhattan. We’ve taken the classic codes of film noir and moved them somewhere gray and everyday like the tax office. It’s about giving a tax office the adrenaline and muscle of the Pentagon. That collision between the ordinary and something as explosive as Dirty Harry is part of the DNA of the series.

	Even when the characters make questionable choices, the series seems more interested in understanding than judging them. Was that important to you?
	

	San José: Above all, we’ve tried to understand them. I don’t think any of the characters in either season is bad.

	Even the alleged tax evaders have understandable interests. The ways they defend them may be wrong, but we’ve tried not to make anyone stupid.

	All the characters in “Celeste,” on both sides of the investigation, are emotionally broken. I don’t think you can hate somebody who isn’t happy when they go to bed. If things aren’t going well for you, I think an embrace comes more naturally than an elbow.

	Elena, how do you convey that emotional vulnerability without tipping into melodrama?

	Trapé: If by sentimental you mean melodramatic, the tone and the way the characters’ feelings emerge are so subtle, delicate and restrained that it’s very difficult for that to happen. That is already very clearly established in Diego’s writing.

	It’s also fundamental that Diego is with me on set every day. Any doubt, any ambiguity, any moment when you ask, “Do we push this further or are we already there?” becomes part of our creative dialogue.



	

					 
									“Celeste” Season 2 Javier Perez Garcia
	



	The series has a particular affinity for losers. What draws you to them?

	San José: We all have a losing side, and not everybody has a winning side. What equalizes all of us is that we all know what it is to lose. Defeat is what makes us connect.

	Both seasons have a special sympathy for losers. We made a heroine out of someone who is clearly looked down on in real life. Tax inspectors are badly regarded in our society.

	The fact that a 62-year-old woman who is a tax inspector can at the same time be Dirty Harry is already a bet on turning the loser into somebody who gets a spotlight in fiction that she doesn’t get in real life. The series is made to weave a nice suit for losers who don’t usually get one.

	The singer Celeste is no longer central to the story. Why keep the title?

	San José: We never attached much importance to the title containing the name of the most important character. “Celeste” for us has become almost more of a color than a figure from music.

	People even sometimes refer to Carmen Machi as Celeste: “Have you seen that series about the inspector, ‘Celeste’?”

	The first season connected with more people than even we expected, so we wanted to keep the same brand.
	

	Elena, after the response to Season 1, what did you want to achieve with the second season?

	Trapé: There’s a solidity to this season that I really like. As the characters gain more volume and nuance, and the plot develops, you enter a universe that keeps expanding. It becomes something more mature.

	One challenge of the first season was establishing its very particular tone. This time we, the crew and Carmen already knew it. That gave us much more room to play.

	Watching it now, I feel we’ve grown. It feels like a very solid season.

	You’ve now made “Celeste” and “Yakarta” together, with Javier Cámara earning an International Emmy nomination last month for the latter. Could there be a “Yakarta 2”?

	San José: My plan, as a viewer, is for Elena to make something without me, because I’d like to see it. The downside of working with Elena for three or four years is that I don’t get to watch things by Elena.

	We’ve made two series together, three seasons in total, and I’m extremely happy with them. But now it’s Elena’s turn to do her own thing.

	If Elena wants to make “Yakarta 2,” it will happen. That depends on Elena.

	Trapé: What I hope neither of us rules out is working together again. Whether it will be “Yakarta 2” or something else, I don’t know.

	San José: I think if Javier Cámara wins the International Emmy, it’s going to be difficult to sit down to dinner without somebody saying, “Why don’t you make a ‘Yakarta 2’?” So let’s make Javier responsible for that.

	This interview has been edited and condensed

schema.headline: ‘Celeste’ Creator Diego San José, Director Elena Trapé on Turning a Tax Inspector Into ‘Dirty Harry’

title: John Rhys-Davies, Diego Boneta Fantasy ‘Starbright’ Boarded by Cappu Films Ahead of Busan Market (EXCLUSIVE)
description: International sales on “Starbright,” Francesco Lucente’s English-language fantasy adventure starring John Rhys-Davies, Diego Boneta and Alexandra Do
body:
International sales on “Starbright,” Francesco Lucente’s English-language fantasy adventure starring John Rhys-Davies, Diego Boneta and Alexandra Dowling, have gone to Cappu Films, which sealed the deal on the eve of the Busan International Film Festival‘s Asian Contents & Film Market.

	Dowling plays Aisling, a young woman who makes a wish on a shooting star and finds herself hunted by people who want its power for themselves. Rhys-Davies is the archangel Raphael, who hides the star’s light inside her heart, and Boneta is Joshua, a stranger with a difficult history who goes on the run with her. Ted Levine, Becky Ann Baker, Gbenga Akinnagbe, Elisabeth Röhm and Christine Ebersole round out the ensemble.
	

	Ludek Drizhal composed the film’s score, which is in contention for the Public Choice Award at this year’s World Soundtrack Awards.


	“We’re delighted to have closed the deal for ‘Starbright’ just ahead of Busan,” said Janice Woo of Cappu Films. “We’re keen to bring more English-language fantasy, action and adventure titles to our catalog, building on our experience with genre films. We really admire what Francesco has created, particularly the music and the emotion it brings to the film. We look forward to introducing ‘Starbright’ to our international buyers.”

	Lucente, who also produced, said he was excited to partner with Cappu to take the film to audiences worldwide. “This film has always been very close to my heart – it’s a story about hope, courage, love, and the belief that even in our darkest moments, something extraordinary can still happen. Cappu’s passion for the film and their strong international reach make them the perfect partner to introduce ‘Starbright’ to new audiences, and I’m thrilled to begin this next chapter of the film’s journey with them.”
	

	Elsewhere on the Cappu slate are “Fox Hunt,” toplined by Tony Leung Chiu-wai, and “Operation Doolittle,” a nine-episode espionage drama set during World War II. The company also handles Erica Xia-Hou’s “Banr,” which played Slamdance; Shan Jiang’s “Ephemera,” a Tribeca title; Stas Mareev’s science-fiction actioner “Overstake”; and “Her Last Laugh,” an Australian comedy-drama from Joy Hopwood.

schema.headline: John Rhys-Davies, Diego Boneta Fantasy ‘Starbright’ Boarded by Cappu Films Ahead of Busan Market (EXCLUSIVE)

title: A Rare David Bowie Self-Portrait — Featuring His Handprints — Is Going on Auction at Sotheby’s
description:
A rare David Bowie self-portrait is going on auction at Sotheby’s, featuring the musician and artist’s own handprints. 

	The 1996 work is part of e
body:
A rare David Bowie self-portrait is going on auction at Sotheby’s, featuring the musician and artist’s own handprints. 

	The 1996 work is part of eight self-portraits Bowie created during a prolific period of painting, all of which were snapped up immediately. Done on paper, the painting emphasizes Bowie’s signature anisocoria and includes two of his actual handprints pressed directly onto the bottom of the composition — making it arguably the closest to a physical trace of the artist a collector could have. 
	

	This particular portrait was gifted by Bowie to his St. Ives gallerist and is now coming to the market for the first time as part of Sotheby’s Modern British and Irish Art Day Auction on Oct. 15. Its price is estimated between £35,000-55,000 ($46,000-72,500). The work is now on public view.


	“There’s something incredibly direct and personal about this self-portrait,” Jen Hardie, Sotheby’s director and senior specialist of modern British and Irish art, tells Variety. “Bowie looks straight out at you, and his own handprints appear on the work itself. It’s bold, colorful and unmistakably Bowie, capturing the same restless creativity that ran through everything he did. It also feels particularly special to see a work like this return to Sotheby’s, a decade after our landmark ‘Bowie/Collector’ sale celebrated the extraordinary breadth of his own collection.”

	Indeed, “Bowie/Collector” in 2016 sold more than 350 works from Bowie’s private collection, bringing in £32.9 million ($43.4 million) and setting 59 artist records. Bowie was an admirer or German Expressionism, dating back to his years in Berlin in the ’70s, and also of School of London artists Leon Kossoff and Frank Auerbach — the influences of which can all be seen in his own work.

title: Bavaria Media Intl. Unveils Mipcom Slate Including German TV Hits ‘Mordach,’ ‘Home-Made Christmas’ and ‘Throughout the Years’ (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Bavaria Media Intl., the distribution arm of Bavaria Film Group, has unveiled a slate of scripted shows ahead of TV market Mipcom, including German
body:
Bavaria Media Intl., the distribution arm of Bavaria Film Group, has unveiled a slate of scripted shows ahead of TV market Mipcom, including German TV hits “Mordach,” “Home-Made Christmas,” “Fanny’s Extraordinary World” and “Throughout the Years.”

	The crime lineup features “Cold Case Diaries,” “Dark Motives,” “Mordach” and “The Wolf Hunt,” while the family-focused content includes “Fanny’s Extraordinary World,” “A Place Called Fatherhood,” “Hearts Along the Baltic Sea,” “Home-Made Christmas” and “Throughout the Years.”
	

	Helge Köhne, head of content sales at Bavaria Media Intl., said, “From talent-led crime titles such as ‘Cold Case Diaries’ and ‘Mordach,’ to proven feel-good and Christmas entertainment ‘Home-Made Christmas,’ and the growing ‘Throughout the Years’ franchise, this new lineup demonstrates the breadth of genre-led content ready for this year’s market, and primed for global audiences. With recognizable talent, strong broadcast performance and stories rooted in universal themes, we are looking forward to introducing Bavaria Media Intl.’s new slate to partners at Mipcom.”


	Crime Slate“Cold Case Diaries”The new season of “Cold Case Diaries” (2 x 90’), coproduced by Hessischer Rundfunk, Degeto and Sommerhaus Filmproduktion, stars Edin Hasanović (“All Quiet on the Western Front,” “Crap Happens”) as chief inspector Hamza Kulina, alongside Melika Foroutan. The German Film Television Award-nominated series reopens unsolved cases in Frankfurt as chief inspector Hamza Kulina (Edin Hasanović) and department head Maryam Azadi (Melika Foroutan) form a relentless duo, investigating fresh leads through old evidence and facing dangerous resistance to bring to light what was left in the dark.
	

	“Mordach”Cross-genre crime thriller “Mordach” (2 x 90’), produced by UFA Fiction and coproduced by ARD Degeto Film and ARD, stars Mehmet Kurtuluş (“Zamanın Kapıları,” “O da Bir Şey mi?”) and Gesine Cukrowski (“Hotel Mondial”). When a BKA undercover agent becomes the prime suspect in a murder he cannot remember committing, he is forced to investigate his own case. Combining contemporary urban crime with an atmospheric Alpine mystery, “Mordach” reached 5.7 million viewers when it premiered on ARD, demonstrating strong audience traction for its distinctive genre proposition.

	“Dark Motives”The latest season of “Dark Motives” (11 x 90’), produced by Filmpool Fiction GmbH for MDR, stars Claudia Michelsen (“The Tower,” “Police Call 110”) as its complex female lead. Set against the rough-edged backdrop of the River Elbe, the harbor and Magdeburg’s housing estates, the female-led crime series tackles family conflict, social divides, economic crime and clan structures through cases rooted in contemporary social issues.

	“The Wolf Hunt”“The Wolf Hunt” (one x 90’) produced by U5 Filmproduktion for ARD Degeto, follows Sara Jahnke, a game warden, who is assigned to track a conspicuous she-wolf and, if necessary, to shoot her. The job drags her back to her home village in Brandenburg, a place she left years ago. What begins as wildlife control turns into a crime story when, deep in the forest, she finds a young woman’s body left for scavengers. Sara follows sign and clue, tests loyalties and refuses to look away until the dead are heard and justice is within reach.

	Feel Good/Family Slate“Fanny’s Extraordinary World”“Fanny’s Extraordinary World” (90’), produced by Neue Schönhauser Filmproduktion for ARD Degeto is a warm, multi-generational family comedy led by acclaimed German actor German Dieter Hallervorden, who plays a charming fraudster Oskar. Fanny, his autistic eight-year-old granddaughter sees the world with bright precision and a sense of wonder. To win her trust, Oskar introduces himself as Professor Krypton instead of admitting he is her long absent grandfather. Combining comedy and emotional depth with neurodiversity representation at its core, the film, which reached over 4 million viewers on its release on ARD, is an uplifting story of family, second chances and connection.
	

	“Home-Made Christmas”“Home-Made Christmas” (90’) produced by Mafilm for ARD Degeto, is a warm-hearted Christmas TV drama starring “Horst Krause,” best known for the popular “Police Chief Krause” films. Set in the cosy rural community of Schönhorst, the film follows innkeeper Horst as he finds a runaway girl and returns her to a neighboring children’s home, where a chance encounter sets a makeshift family on an unexpected journey towards belonging. Having reached 5 million viewers when the film premiered on ARD and a 17.7% market share, “Home-Made Christmas” is a feel-good Christmas story, primed for family viewing.

	“Throughout the Years”“Throughout the Years” (90’), produced by UFA Fiction, is a star-studded Christmas romance featuring Charly Hübner (“The Lives of Others”), Maria Simon (“The Silent Revolution”), Klaus Steinbacher (“The Ibiza Affair”) and Sinje Irslinger (“We Children from Bahnhof Zoo”). The first instalment reached 3.92 million viewers and a 16.1% market share on German national television, including an 11.3% share among 14-49-year-olds, demonstrating particularly strong younger-audience appeal. Part 2 is planned for Christmas 2026, with Part 3 currently in development.

	“A Place Called Fatherhood”“A Place Called Fatherhood” (90’), produced by Pyjama Pictures GmbH for ARD Degeto, stars David Rott (“Die Toten von Salzburg”) and breakout talent Sabrina Amali (“Dogs of Berlin,” “Skylines”) in a warm, contemporary family drama about co-parenting and the realities of blended families. The story follows high-flying Frankfurt sales professional Jonas, as he re-evaluates his priorities when his daughter Laila asks for more time and closeness. Moving to Hamburg, Jonas discovers A Bed for Dad, a welcoming home for separated parents and their children, where he begins to rediscover the everyday realities of fatherhood.

	“Hearts Along the Baltic Sea”“Hearts Along the Baltic Sea” (90’), produced by sabotage films GmbH for ARD Degeto, is a feel-good romantic drama for multigenerational audiences, starring Jennifer Ulrich (“The Wave”) and marking the debut of writer-director Joana Vogdt. As a 90-minute format designed for all ages, the story follows Hamburg carpenter Eva Jensen as she heads to the Baltic coast to take over a small woodworking shop, only to find herself caught in a long-standing family conflict and a rivalry with kitesurfer Christian, who is competing for the same workshop.

title: How ‘Dying to Survive’ Director Wen Muye Turned a Cook’s War Into $342 Million China Smash ‘Once Upon a Time in the Middle East’: ‘I Never Think About Social Issues in Advance’
description: Xu Fu went to the Middle East for the money. The Shenyang cook, played by Shen Teng in “Once Upon a Time in the Middle East,” takes the head-chef jo
body:
Xu Fu went to the Middle East for the money. The Shenyang cook, played by Shen Teng in “Once Upon a Time in the Middle East,” takes the head-chef job at the Dragon Restaurant because the pay could help clear his family’s debts. When war breaks out, he is shaken from his sleep and runs for an air-raid shelter.

	Director Wen Muye says he never stopped to think about how grand the film’s backdrop was.


	“Although the backdrop may seem very large, for a specific little person – an ordinary person – this is a very concrete predicament that he has to face,” Wen tells Variety. “We try not to consider how grand it is; we only consider how great an impact it has on the character.”
	

	Chinese audiences have followed that cook a long way. Since opening on Aug. 11, the film has grossed RMB2.29 billion ($342 million) in China, making it the third-highest-grossing Chinese film of 2026. It is Wen’s follow-up to “Dying to Survive” and “Nice View.”

	The idea came from a news report and from the experiences of real Chinese cooks who run restaurants in the region.

	“For me, Xu Fu is still an ordinary person, an ordinary chef,” Wen says. “What he goes through is in fact connected to the work he does as a chef, the food he makes, and his relationship with war. There is room there to express the relationship between war and peace.”

	Shen is one of China’s biggest stars and is closely tied to comedy. Wen says that reputation was part of his thinking when he cast him in a war drama.

	“But the fundamental premise was first and foremost that Shen Teng was very suitable for the role of Xu Fu. In my mind, Xu Fu is a middle-aged Northeastern chef with a sense of humor, and Shen Teng is comparatively very well suited to the role,” he says. “At the same time, he has the ability and talent for comedic performance, which naturally brings a certain sense of ease to some of the heavier themes.”
	

	With restaurant manager Ma Junsheng (Jiang Qiming), Xu Fu turns the failing restaurant into a going concern. Once the fighting reaches the city, it becomes a shelter for people trapped by the war. Wen wanted to follow an ordinary cook through a conflict, and the restaurant came with the job.

	“At first, it exists and prospers; later, it disappears from the protagonist’s view; and in the end, after the protagonist has grown old and returns to the Chinese restaurant, he sees that it is still standing there,” Wen says. “This is in fact a symbol of a certain kind of peace.”

	For much of the story, Xu Fu looks out for himself and treats the war as someone else’s problem. That changes when Ma is killed rescuing children whom terrorists are forcing to become suicide bombers. Wen says he didn’t set out to ask what ordinary people owe one another.

	“I think it is driven by human nature – whether Xu Fu or Ma Junsheng, these characters are driven by instinct,” he says.

	To prepare, the team interviewed many people working in the region. They spoke to cooks, to workers from a wide range of trades and to locals who had lived through the war. Wen then tried to put himself in each character’s place at each moment.

	“I never think about social issues in advance. What I actually want to tell is the story of specific people,” Wen says. “War and peace are certainly one theme of this film, but if you always write characters with that idea in mind, there will actually be problems.”

	Omar Sherif plays Seif, a Kurdish Iraqi orphan who becomes Xu Fu’s apprentice. Aarif Lee makes a special appearance as Tony, a Chinese American private in the U.S. Army, and Sherif Sobhy plays Zaid, a civil servant and restaurant shareholder whom the war drives to seek revenge.

	Wen wrote the screenplay with Lang Qunli and Zhong Wei, his co-writer on “Dying to Survive” and “Nice View.” Ning Hao is executive producer; Wen joined Ning’s Dirty Monkeys’ 72 Transformations Film Project in 2016. Wen studied under Tian Zhuangzhuang at the Beijing Film Academy, and “Dying to Survive” won him best new director at the 2018 Golden Horse Awards.

	Well Go USA Entertainment releases the film in North America on Oct. 9.

title: ‘Avatar: Seven Havens’ Takes the Franchise in an Intriguing, Postapocalyptic New Direction: TV Review
description: This summer, the Avatar franchise reintroduced itself by revisiting its most iconic character: Aang, the namesake of “Avatar: The Last Airbender” an
body:
This summer, the Avatar franchise reintroduced itself by revisiting its most iconic character: Aang, the namesake of “Avatar: The Last Airbender” and the original protagonist of a story now in its third decade. For its next act, the Avatar Studios imprint — overseen by original series creators Michael Dante DiMartino and Bryan Konietzko and tasked with expanding the Nickelodeon children’s show into a multimedia enterprise — faces the tougher task of introducing new protagonists and ideas while preserving Avatar’s core appeal.
	

	The Paramount+ series “Avatar: Seven Havens” quite literally brings the saga into the future. Specifically, it’s been more than two centuries since the conclusion of “Avatar: The Legend of Korra,” the sequel series that wrapped its run in 2014. “Seven Havens,” also created by DiMartino and Konietzko, uses the leap forward to fundamentally alter the composition of this fictional world. (Longtime animation hand Ethan Spaulding, who executive produces, and co-executive producer Sehaj Sethi also form the creative team.) Gone are the four nations, corresponding to the elements, who coexisted in harmony that was disrupted and then, episode by episode, restored. In their place is a world reduced to a wasteland by an environmental cataclysm, supposedly caused by Korra herself. The namesake havens are city-states that offer refuge from sandstorms, bandits and other threats — and the Avatar, a quasi-messianic figure able to “bend” all four elements, is a stigmatized bogeyman who hasn’t appeared for generations.


	Enter Pavi (Saheli Khan), an orphan from the haven of Ellora who spends her days scrounging for food, trying to keep her multi-element bending abilities under wraps and talking to the inanimate objects she keeps around in lieu of friends. Pavi’s name is an indication of another way “Seven Havens” expands the Avatar mythos: by incorporating South Asian culture to the universe’s pre-existing blend of Chinese, Japanese, Inuit and other influences. Pavi’s favorite snack are the kachoris knowingly left out by a local shopkeeper, herself voiced by veteran actor Sakina Jaffrey. Food, in general, is an object of concern for “Seven Havens”: Mochi, kimchi jjigae and bitter melon are all cited by name in the first few episodes alone.
	

	But an equally significant update “Seven Havens” makes to the cosmology is in how the show depicts the natural world — always a preoccupation for a story grounded in air, earth, fire and water. The “Harshlands” that surround Ellora are filled with rocks, sand and a strange, haunted beauty. The color palette of “Seven Havens” is warmer than prior Avatar series, favoring the oranges and pinks of an almost Saharan expanse. (The music, from franchise stalwart Jeremy Zuckerman, also sets “Seven Havens” apart aurally with a more electronic sound.) There are cats with monkey tails, and camels that roll up in a ball like armadillos! With a postapocalyptic landscape indifferent and even hostile to human needs, “Seven Havens” reminded me of “Scavengers Reign,” the magnificent yet short-lived series on HBO Max. Hopefully, having the IP tie-in will give “Seven Havens” more time to explore its environment.

	And “Seven Havens” could use some time to grow. Pavi is a younger hero than even 12-year-old Aang, perhaps an attempt to introduce Avatar to a new generation of kids where the movie was more of a service to pre-existing fans. Shy, nerdy and a pacifist by nature, Pavi has a personality, if one that’s still in formation. She’s mentored by Jae (Major Curda), a member of Ellora’s municipal Bending Brigade, and his captain Karthik (Akshay Khanna), who has a more optimistic view of the Avatar’s potential than those that blame her for ending the world. In the six episodes provided to critics, this crew hasn’t quite coalesced into a unified team, but “Seven Havens” successfully cultivates enough curiosity about how its world works to buy some time.

	“Seven Havens” introduces another quirk to the Avatar legend I’m forbidden from disclosing, though it takes some pressure off Pavi as Karthik explores his theory that the Avatar can help revive the dying art of bending. (There are fewer benders born to each successive generation, we’re told, even as manipulating the elements is a vital defense against an onslaught of lightning and wind.) Combined with the imagery and an expanded pool of references, “Seven Havens” successfully makes clear that it’s a new and different kind of Avatar series, while maintaining the transportive world-building that’s helped the franchise endure.
	

	The first three episodes of “Avatar: Seven Havens” are now streaming on Paramount+, with remaining episodes airing weekly in batches of three on Fridays.

schema.headline: ‘Avatar: Seven Havens’ Takes the Franchise in an Intriguing, Postapocalyptic New Direction: TV Review

title: SkyShowtime’s ‘The Homicide Unit,’ From Warner Bros., and Iceland’s ‘Fjord’ Boarded by Reinvent Yellow Sales (EXCLUSIVE)
description: SkyShowtime’s “The Homicide Unit” produced by Warner Bros. International Television Production (WBITVP) Sweden, and Iceland’s “Fjord” have been adde
body:
SkyShowtime’s “The Homicide Unit” produced by Warner Bros. International Television Production (WBITVP) Sweden, and Iceland’s “Fjord” have been added to Reinvent Yellow Sales’ Mipcom slate.The two crime shows feature top female investigators played by internationally acclaimed Nordic theps, Swedish star Pernilla August (“Blackwater,” ”Star Wars: Episode I – The Phantom Menace”) and Iceland’s Anita Briem (“The Tudors,” “The Minister”, “As Long As We Live”) respectively.
	

	The shows see Reinvent Yellow, one year after the merger of Yellow Film Studios and REinvent, keeping premium Nordic shows at its core while gradually expanding into English-language titles.


	Created by Gunnar A. K. Järvstad (“Top Dog”), the eight-parter “The Homicide Unit” (“Riksmord”) is inspired by a real-life travelling elite unit as they help the local police untangle complex murder cases. Making up the top cop team are August (who plays the chief ‘Ib’) Jonas Karlsson (“Riding in Darkness,” “Quick”), Alexander Abdallah (“Snabba Cash,” “Paradise City”), and Nina Zanjani (“Beck,” “Agent Hamilton”). Set to premiere in March 2027, the show was co-produced by SkyShowtime, TV4 in Sweden, with regional backers Film i Skåne, Film i Dalarna and Filmpool Nord.

	Just as the varied landscape of Sweden’s mighty forest to its picturesque coastline enhance the storyline of “The Homicide Unit,” the striking and atmospheric nature of Northern Iceland plays an integral part of the tense thriller “Fjord.”



	

					Fjord
									Courtesy of Reinvent Yellow
	



	Co-created by Briem with writer-director Constantine Paraskevopoulos, the six-part series in English and Icelandic language turns on Ranna (Briem), who follows her fiancé Sveinn (Pääru Oja) back to Iceland after the collapse of their London gallery. Struggling to fit in, Ranna becomes obsessed with a decade-old disappearance of a choir teacher and starts a podcast about the case. She ends up uncovering the town’s secrets and truths about herself. “Fjord” is a crime series where the real danger isn’t violence but proximity: living too close to the same people, with shared histories and too much to lose,” said Paraskevopoulos is a statement.Produced by Iceland’s Guðný Guðjónsdóttir Sara Djeddou Baldursdóttir (Projects) with Belgium’s Lunanime, for local streamer Síminn, “Fjord” will premiere later this year.Reinvent Yellow Sales’ chief sales officer in charge of marketing Helene Aurø said that “with distinctive creative voices, strong casts and stories that resonate beyond their borders,” both series “showcase the strength and range of Nordic storytelling.”
	

	Crime Focus

	Other such titles in the sales outlet’s Mipcom slate include “Nora Sand: Devil’s Plan”, third adaptation of Lone Theil’s best-selling novels from Norwegian creators Arne Berggren and Kristine Berg of Shuuto Arctic. The two first series “Fatal Crossing” and “The Pushover” played strongly internationally, with recent sales closed notably with MHZ Networks for North America, and Global Series Network/Walter Presents for the U.K. and Ireland. Commissioned by DR in Denmark and TV4 in Sweden, “Nora Sand: Devil’s Plan” will be delivered later this year.

	Complementing the crime offers are three Finnish series produced by Reinvent Yellow’s partner Yellow Film & TV: “Helsinki Tallinn,” “The Truth,” and “Port Poison,” and two high-end shows, part of a three-title deal with Nordisk Film Production: Prime Video’s first Danish Original “Snake Killer” starring Pilou Asbæk, and TV2 Norway’s cosy crime “Sogn Murders” starring Kristofer Hivju.Rounding out Reinvent Yellow’s Mipcom scripted slate is the hospital drama “The New Nurses” season 8, part of TV2 Denmark, SF Studios Production hit franchise, to be delivered late 2026.

	“Our slate reflects a clear strategy: building on our Nordic strengths while expanding our English-language ambitions,” seasoned Danish executive Aurø told Variety. “Since the merger with Yellow Film & TV [a year ago], we have accelerated our work with Nordic titles and made good progress on the English-language side, with several exciting projects in development. It is an evolution of our identity, grounded in strong local storytelling with the ambition to reach international audiences.”

	Commenting on buyers’ behavior, ahead of Mipcom, she said “crime, thriller, survival and disaster and action remains the most sought-after genre, and buyers are still acquiring, although they are selective. A familiar genre helps open the door, but a series needs a distinctive voice, compelling characters and a clear audience to stand out. For us, the focus is on stories that combine that appeal with something fresh, giving buyers a strong reason to commit.”
